title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence
statement: You get an integer array `nums`. Choose a subsequence of it (drop any number of elements, possibly none, and keep the rest in their original order) whose consecutive elements all differ by one common value; that common step may be positive, negative or zero. Return the greatest possible length of such a subsequence. Any two elements already form one, so the answer is always at least 2.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every pair as the first two terms and then scanning for the rest takes O(n³). Instead, think like the longest increasing subsequence: every arithmetic subsequence ends somewhere and has a step. If we know, for each earlier index `j` and each step, the longest progression ending at `j`, then appending `nums[i]` extends exactly the progression whose step is `nums[i] - nums[j]`.

## Approach

1. Keep `dp[i]`, a map from a step `diff` to the length of the longest progression with that step ending at index `i`. Start `best` at 2, since any pair counts.
2. For each `i`, open an empty map and look at every earlier `j`.
3. Let `diff = nums[i] - nums[j]`. The progression ending at `j` with that step (or just the single element `nums[j]`, length 1) grows by one: `length = (dp[j].get(diff) ?? 1) + 1`.
4. Store `length` in `dp[i]` under `diff` and update `best`.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 6, 9, 12]`. At `i = 1`, `j = 0` gives step 3 and length 2. At `i = 2`, `j = 0` gives step 6, length 2, then `j = 1` finds step 3 stored at index 1 with length 2, so `dp[2]` gets step 3 with length 3. At `i = 3`, `j = 2` finds step 3 with length 3 at index 2, giving length 4, so `best = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each pair `(j, i)` does a constant amount of map work.
- Space: O(n²): each index stores at most one entry per earlier index.

## Pitfalls

- The step can be negative or zero; a map (or an offset array of size 1001) handles every step from -500 to 500.
- A pair with no earlier progression still has length 2, so the default before adding one is 1, not 0.
- Overwriting `dp[i]` for a repeated step is safe: a later `j` with the same value can end every progression an earlier one could, so its length is never smaller.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp` | `dp[i]` maps a step to the longest progression with that step ending at `i` |
| `best` | longest length found so far |
| `i` | index of the element being appended |
| `j` | index of the previous element in the progression |
| `diff` | the step `nums[i] - nums[j]` |
| `length` | the progression length ending at `i` with step `diff` |
